title: Investigatio motuum, quibus laminae et virgae elasticae contremiscunt

deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler's equation for transverse vibration of a uniform elastic rod. Writing u = s/a and ω = a/f, the spatial mode is y = α e^{s/f} + β e^{-s/f} + γ sin(s/f) + δ cos(s/f).

Part 1 (end of Scholion 3, free–free rod, first mode). For the free–free rod Euler takes ω ≈ 3ϱ with ϱ = π/2; the exact root of cos ω cosh ω = 1 is ω = 4.730. He normalises the mode as
 y = e^{uω} + e^{ω(1-u)} + (1-e^ω) sin uω + (1+e^ω) cos uω.
Its slope (per unit ω) is
 y' = e^{uω} - e^{ω(1-u)} + (1-e^ω) cos uω - (1+e^ω) sin uω.
- At E (u=0): y' = 2(1-e^ω). This was done on the previous page.
- At F (u=1): y' = e^ω - 1 + (1-e^ω) cos ω - (1+e^ω) sin ω. Use sin ω ≈ -1 and cos ω ≈ 2/(e^ω+e^{-ω}) ≈ 2e^{-ω}, and drop e^{-ω}. This gives y' = 2(e^ω-1). The end slopes are therefore equal and opposite, so the angles EeL and FfM are equal: the mode is symmetric.
- At the midpoint O (u=1/2): the hyperbolic terms cancel, leaving y' = (1-e^ω) cos(ω/2) - (1+e^ω) sin(ω/2). With the crude values cos(ω/2) = -1/√2 and sin(ω/2) = 1/√2 this gives -√2. Euler remarks that an exact calculation would give 0, so the tangent at o is parallel to the axis.
- This remark is correct. The symmetric free–free modes satisfy tan(ω/2) = (1-e^ω)/(1+e^ω) = -tanh(ω/2), which makes y'(1/2) vanish exactly. The residual -√2 comes from replacing ω by exactly 3π/2. That small angle error is multiplied by terms of size e^ω ≈ 113, and -√2 is in any case tiny compared with end slopes of size about 2e^ω ≈ 220.
- He adds that the higher modes ω ≈ 5ϱ, 7ϱ, 9ϱ can be treated the same way.

Part 2 (start of Case II, §23). Problem: one end E is free, the other end F is pinned to a stylus about which the rod may turn freely (hinged/simply supported). Find all regular (normal-mode) vibrations.
- Free end s=0: y'' = 0 and y''' = 0. This gives α+β-δ = 0 and α-β-γ = 0, so γ = α-β and δ = α+β, as in Case I.
- Pinned end s=a: y = 0 and y'' = 0. This condition is carried out on the next page and leads to tan ω = tanh ω, the classical free–pinned frequency equation.
errors: Sign/term slip at u=1: the text says 'ob cos ω = -1 et sin ω = 2/e^ω'. This swaps sine and cosine relative to the previous page (sin ω = -1, cos ω = 2/(e^ω+e^{-ω})). Only the previous page's values yield the stated result 2(e^ω-1): e^ω - 1 + (1-e^ω)·2e^{-ω} + (1+e^ω) ≈ 2e^ω - 2. With the values as printed, the expression would be ≈ -2 - 2e^{-ω}·(...), not 2(e^ω-1). So this is a printing or editorial slip; the conclusion is right.
The midpoint slope -√2 is an artefact of taking ω = 3π/2 exactly. Euler himself flags this, correctly stating that the exact value is 0. It is not an error in the theory.

ideas.what: Symmetry check of the first free–free mode via end slopes and a horizontal tangent at the midpoint, with error control from the approximation ω ≈ 3π/2.
ideas.modern_name: Symmetric normal mode of a free–free Euler–Bernoulli beam (tan(ω/2) + tanh(ω/2) = 0)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Daniel Bernoulli and Euler (1740s–1770s); standardized by Rayleigh (Theory of Sound)
ideas.where_published: E526 itself (Acta Acad. Sci. Petrop. 1779/1782); free–free frequencies also in earlier Euler work (Methodus inveniendi 1744, Additamentum I)

ideas.what: Boundary conditions y''=0, y'''=0 at a free end and y=0, y''=0 at a pinned end, leading to the free–pinned frequency equation tan ω = tanh ω.
ideas.modern_name: Free–hinged (free–simply supported) beam boundary conditions and characteristic equation
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler and D. Bernoulli; analysed historically by Truesdell (1960)
ideas.where_published: E526 §23ff.; discussed in Truesdell, The Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies 1638–1788

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine numerical check of the mode shape and the setup of a standard boundary-value case. Euler's beam-vibration analysis in E526 is well documented, notably by Truesdell. The only noteworthy item is a minor sin/cos slip in the print.
transcription_corrections: The previous page's 'ω = 3,9 circiter' should read 'ω = 3ϱ circiter' (ϱ = right angle, π/2).
On this page the image indeed reads 'cof. ω = -1 et fin. ω = 2/e^ω'. This is faithful to the print, but the print is inconsistent with the previous page.
The '- - -' leaders in the previous page's formulas are typographic fillers, not minus signs: y = e^{uω} + e^{ω(1-u)} + ...
